_comment: Perceived-latency budgets for gateway-backed flows, stated from the vault owner's seat. The gateway's MACHINE-cost budgets (request p99, RSS, event-loop lag, fsyncs per write, idle churn) already live in packages/server/benchmarks/low-end-budgets.json and stay there — this file is the symptom layer above them. See README.md for the status vocabulary and the year-3 volume table. Ratcheted tighten-only via PERF_BUDGET_SOURCES.

sendToFirstToken.volume: empty vault, no conversation history — 13 runs of 25-30 sampled turns, each after 5 discarded warmups, provider held constant at zero think time
sendToFirstToken.probe: scripts/perf/send-to-first-token.mjs — drives a real runAcpTurn against the scripted packages/server/src/acp/backends/acp/fake-acp-harness.mjs (--mode=normal) and times t0 (send) → first `assistant.delta`. PARTIAL BY CONSTRUCTION, and this entry says so rather than implying the whole interval is fenced. IN the span: harness process spawn, the ACP initialize handshake, session/new, session/prompt dispatch, and the stream translation in packages/server/src/acp/backends/acp/backend.ts. OUT of it: the HTTP/SSE conversation route in front of runAcpTurn, every client (no renderer, no frame, no composer), and a real provider's own time to first token — that last one is deliberately excluded, because it is the provider's number and not a regression this repo can fix. STILL UNMEASURED: the route + client half, which needs the desktop/web e2e mock gateway to serve a fixed-delay SSE turn plus a client-side first-token marker to observe; the `sendToFirstToken` entries in desktop.json and web.json remain unmeasured for exactly that reason.

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 cpus, shared container under concurrent sibling load (load average 3.3-4.5 of 4 during the noisiest runs); @centraid/server consumed from its built dist
_provenance.note: MEASURED — and what it replaces is NO NUMBER AT ALL. Before this the product's most-felt latency had no rig: tests/perf/harness-turn.perf.test.ts measures 2,000 registry dispatches against a stubbed runTurn, so it never spawns a harness, never speaks ACP, and could not see this interval. The stub the old probe text asked for turned out to already exist (fake-acp-harness.mjs, the ACP backend suite's fixture); the missing piece was a rig pointing at it. Thirteen independent runs of 25-30 samples put per-run p95 between 53.4 ms on an idle container and 123.0 ms under concurrent load, while the per-run MEDIAN barely moved (47.9-69.5 ms) — so the spread is host contention on the process spawn, not variance in the path itself. Every observed* value above records the WORST run seen, never the friendliest. The number is dominated by node process spawn plus the JSON-RPC handshake, which is the honest shape of a first turn. READ IT AS A LOWER BOUND on what the vault owner feels: it fences a gateway-side regression — a slower spawn, an added handshake round trip, a blocking step inserted before the prompt goes out — not the whole perceived interval.
_provenance.headroom: ~3.3x worst observed p95 (~2x the worst single sample), in the same grammar as requestToFirstByte above. Sized against the CONTENDED measurement on purpose, because a shared CI runner IS the contended case: a ceiling seeded from the idle 53 ms p95 would fence runner jitter rather than a regression, and a gate that flakes is a gate that gets widened. The ratchet is tighten-only, so this can only come DOWN — re-seed it from a real distribution on the lane that runs it.

reconnectToFresh.volume: YEAR-3: 50,000 replica rows (schedule.task) walked through the windowed bootstrap route in 3 pages of 20,000, then 25 commits written while the client is disconnected and replayed against its stale cursor
reconnectToFresh.probe: tests/scale/replica-reconnect.scale.test.ts — times the reconnect REQUEST to the frame that carries every missed change. IN the span: connection setup, cursor parse, shape rebuild, and the projection of the missed delta. OUT of it: how long the owner was away, which is unbounded and is not the gateway's to own. Page ONE's watermark is used as the resume cursor because that is what the bootstrap continuation token pins the client's later delta to.

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2; in-process serve() gateway over loopback HTTP
_provenance.note: MEASURED, and what it replaces is NO NUMBER AT ALL — this entry was `unmeasured` with `probe: "NONE TODAY"` because nothing in the repo timed the change-stream resume path. It does now: at the declared year-3 volume a returning device is fresh again in ~60 ms. The first `change` frame WAS the fresh frame in all three runs — 25 missed commits fit inside one page (the route's default limit is 1,000 changes), so first-frame and fully-caught-up are the same instant here and the rig publishes both. THE HONEST CAVEAT: 25 offline commits is a realistic phone-in-a-pocket gap, not a fortnight away; a client whose backlog exceeds one page walks several pages and pays per page. The rig fences the common case and would catch the regression that matters — a resume that starts scanning the vault instead of the change log.
_provenance.headroom: ~3.6x the worst observed (68.7 ms). Sized against the shared-container measurement on purpose, in the same grammar as the other entries here; tighten-only, so re-seed it downward once the nightly scale lane has a real distribution.

requestToFirstByte.volume: TWO LANES against one ceiling. FLOOR: empty vault, 60 serial GETs of /centraid/_apps in a forked child. VOLUME: a year-3-shaped vault — 25,007 domain rows (5,000 core_party, 10,000 photos as content+asset pairs) plus 200 conversations x 12 journal turns and the replica change log those inserts produced — 30 serial GETs of the same route in-process (#883 C1).
requestToFirstByte.probe: tests/perf/gateway-request.perf.test.ts (empty-vault floor) + tests/perf/gateway-request-volume.perf.test.ts (year-3-shaped vault). Both assert this ceiling, so one number now fences the transport regression AND the scale regression.

_provenance.host: darwin arm64, gateway in a forked child (tests/perf/fixtures/gateway-idle-server.mjs)
_provenance.note: Pre-existing measurement, restated here in owner terms and NOT re-derived. Ceiling is ~3x observed. The volume is EMPTY — this number says nothing about a year-3 vault, and the honest reading is that it fences a transport regression, not a scale one. packages/server/benchmarks/low-end-budgets.json holds the matching machine-cost ceiling (requestP99Ms 250) for the low-end host profile. `_provenanceAtVolume` below is the half this note said was missing.

_provenanceAtVolume.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2; gateway IN PROCESS (the seed has to reach the vault it serves), so these are a floor relative to the forked-child lane
_provenanceAtVolume.note: MEASURED at volume, and the finding is that the CORE ROUTES ARE VOLUME-INSENSITIVE: /centraid/_apps answers in 26-34 ms p95 over a 25,007-row vault, against 40 ms p95 on an empty vault in the older forked-child lane — inside the run-to-run spread of the two hosts, not a scale signal. That is the honest, and mildly boring, answer to the question the empty-vault caveat kept parked: this route does not read domain rows, so it cannot degrade with them. What the same rig also publishes, UNGATED, is the lane that does: one windowed replica bootstrap page (window=200) over the same vault costs 152-185 ms p95. Volume shows up on the routes that read rows, and the budget now says which is which instead of implying the whole surface was fenced.
_provenanceAtVolume.headroom: none added — the ceiling stays at ~3x the WORST of the two lanes (the 40 ms empty-vault observation). Tightening it to ~3x the volume observation would fence the forked-child lane's own host noise rather than a regression, and this file is tighten-only, so a ceiling that has to come back up is a ceiling that needs an approvedDeviation.

coreRouteP95Ms.volume: TWO LANES against one ceiling, 30 serial requests per core route identity in each: an EMPTY vault in a forked child, and a year-3-shaped vault (25,007 domain rows + 2,400 journal turns) in process (#883 C1)

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2; in-process gateway over a 25,007-row vault
_provenance.note: MEASURED at volume — before this the entry carried three ceilings and no provenance at all, derived from an empty-vault run on another host. All three routes stay under 35 ms p95 on a year-3-shaped vault; the spread between runs (8.7-34.1 ms on the same route) is container contention, which is why the ceilings are not tightened toward the observation. Keeping one ceiling per identity rather than three different ones is deliberate: these are the three routes a client hits before it can show anything, and a differentiated ceiling would encode today's implementation rather than the owner's experience.
_provenance.headroom: ~3.5x the worst observed at volume (34.1 ms) and ~3x the empty-vault observation (40 ms) the older lane still asserts against. Tighten-only.

gatewayColdStartMs.volume: TWO LANES against one ceiling: fork to authenticated ready message on an EMPTY vault, and an in-process reopen of a SEEDED year-3-shaped vault directory (25,007 domain rows) from disk (#883 C1)
gatewayColdStartMs.probe: tests/perf/gateway-request.perf.test.ts (empty-vault fork) + tests/perf/gateway-request-volume.perf.test.ts (reopen of the seeded directory)

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2
_provenance.note: MEASURED on a SEEDED vault, which is the question this key exists to answer: does a full vault make the gateway slower to open? Reopening a 25,007-row vault from disk — mounting the plane, installing the bundled apps, re-arming the services — takes 0.55-0.81 s. The empty-vault fork lane measures process spawn plus the same boot and carries the same ceiling; neither observation is close to it, and the ceiling is deliberately left generous because a cold start also pays for whatever the host's page cache does not have. Tighten-only.
_provenance.headroom: ~6x the worst seeded reopen (809 ms). The in-process reopen skips node process spawn, which the forked-child lane pays for; the ceiling covers both.

year3RestoreSeconds.volume: 10 GiB of CAS bytes + 95,640 FK-checked rows (90,640 core_content_item + 5,000 core_party)

_provenance.note: MEASURED — this replaces a guess. Before #659 the largest restore the repo had ever executed was ~160 MiB, and the year-3 restore time was unmeasured. A 10 GiB vault comes back in 55 s on local NVMe. CI disks and a network provider are materially slower, hence a ceiling of ~3x observed. NOTE the asymmetry: taking the snapshot costs 152 s, nearly 3x the restore — chunking + AEAD on the way in is the expensive direction.
_provenance.headroom: ~3.2x observed (local-disk measurement, CI/network provider will be slower)

restoreForeignKeyCheckMs.volume: 95,640 rows in the restored vault.db (73 MB file), year-3 row counts
restoreForeignKeyCheckMs.probe: tests/scale/restore-10gib.scale.test.ts — timed alone on a freshly opened connection so neither pragma warms the other's page cache

_provenance.note: MEASURED, and the answer is reassuring: foreign_key_check — the O(rows) full-table walk that packages/backup/src/wal-restore.ts runs inside every restore, and the suspected year-3 cliff — costs 21 ms at year-3 row volume. integrity_check is 37x more expensive at 785 ms, and BOTH together are ~1.5% of the 55 s restore. The honesty check in the restore path is not the thing to optimise. Ceiling is generous on purpose: it fences a genuine cliff (a missing parent index turning the walk quadratic), not runner jitter.

fiveVaultFootprint.volume: 5 mounted vaults = 10 SQLite handles (year-3 household: Personal auto-founded per #603, plus one shared or personal vault per member)

_provenance.note: MEASURED. The reservations are now FLAT in vault count: five vaults under one host budget reserve 32,768,000 B of page cache — exactly one default vault's worth — where the pre-#659 per-file constants would have reserved 163,840,000 B, a 5x reduction. Every one of the 10 handles still gets 3.28 MB, well above the 512 KiB floor. THE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS: reservations are not residency. Each additional mounted vault still costs ~10.1 MB of RSS at idle (connection state + bootstrap DDL, not the page cache, which SQLite fills lazily), so resident memory is still linear in vault count even though the budget is not. Measured on idle, freshly bootstrapped vaults that were never read — treat 10.1 MB as a floor.
_provenance.headroom: none — the ceilings ARE the host totals (DEFAULT_VAULT_FOOTPRINT), not observed + slack

compositeLoadFactor.volume: 20 ops each on five HTTP lanes (windowed replica bootstrap, Notes search, Notes create-note, blob staging, Atlas ref-search) at 2 in flight per lane, plus 128 harness turn dispatches and a 200-automation missed-window scan — run once one-lane-at-a-time (solo) and once all together (composite), against ONE real serve() gateway with the eight bundled apps installed and an empty vault

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container under sibling agent load; node v22.22.2; WORKER_MAX_CONCURRENT resolves to 2 because isConstrainedWorkerHost() classifies a 4-core host as constrained
_provenance.observedWorstLaneIdentity: write (Notes create-note — journalled command + receipt, through an app-engine worker)
_provenance.note: MEASURED, and what it replaces is NO NUMBER AT ALL — before this rig every perf/scale rig in the repo measured one dimension against an otherwise idle gateway. The headline is reassuring: running the whole household together costs about the same WALL CLOCK as running the lanes one after another (0.75-1.05x), so the gateway is genuinely overlapping work rather than serializing behind one lock. THE FINDING THAT IS NOT reassuring is the per-lane spread: the cheapest lane (Atlas ref-search, ~5 ms solo) degrades 27-66x under composition, to 217-361 ms. That is the app-engine worker spawns (create-note and search each spawn a capped worker thread, and this host admits only 2 at once) taking the CPU away from an in-gateway read. It is a fairness observation, not a refusal or a correctness failure — every op completed and nothing was shed. Per-lane latency ratios are therefore PUBLISHED BY THE RIG BUT NOT GATED: a ratio over a ~5 ms denominator fences scheduler noise, and a gate that flakes is a gate that gets widened.
_provenance.headroom: ceilingThroughputFactor ~1.9x the worst observed (1.05); ceilingWorstLaneP95Ms ~3x the worst observed (1147.5 ms). Both sized against the CONTENDED measurements on purpose — a shared CI runner IS the contended case. Tighten-only: re-seed from a real distribution once the nightly lane has one.

refSearchUnderComposition.volume: the Atlas `ref-search` lane of the composite rig — 20 GETs of /centraid/_vault/atlas/browse/ref-search at 2 in flight, run WHILE the four other HTTP lanes, 128 harness turn dispatches and a 200-automation missed-window scan are in flight against the same gateway
refSearchUnderComposition.probe: tests/scale/composite-load.scale.test.ts — the `browse` lane's composite p95, asserted in the rig body. Named separately from `compositeLoadFactor.ceilingWorstLaneP95Ms` because that ceiling only ever fences whichever lane happens to be slowest (the write lane, today), so a ref-search regression could double before the worst-lane gate noticed.

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2; in-process serve() gateway, empty vault, eight bundled apps
_provenance.note: MEASURED after #883 C2 correlated the blob egress reference CTE (packages/vault/src/blob/read.ts): the revision-chain predicate used to seed its recursive walk from `SELECT current_content_id FROM core_document` — the whole library — on every byte request, and now walks from the requested page toward the document head through rung 7's core_link endpoint indexes. This entry is the ref-search half of that composition asked for by #883 C2 item 4; the read lane is fenced here rather than only through the worst-lane ceiling.
_provenance.headroom: ~3x the worst of three observations on a contended shared container, the convention the neighbouring entries use. Tighten-only.

soakDegradation.volume: one long-lived serve() gateway driven in a loop; each cycle is 3 ops on each of five lanes (windowed replica bootstrap, Notes search, Notes create-note, 64 KiB blob staging, Atlas ref-search) at 2 in flight per lane. A 10-minute run is 483 cycles / 7,245 ops / ~1,450 notes and ~1,450 CAS objects accumulated. The first 3 cycles are discarded as warm-up.
soakDegradation.probe: tests/scale/long-run-soak.scale.test.ts (CENTRAID_SOAK_MINUTES; defaults to 0.75 so the rig always runs on the nightly scale lane, weekly lane sets hours)

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container under sibling agent load; node v22.22.2
_provenance.runs: one 10-minute run (483 cycles, 7,245 ops) plus one 0.75-minute run (41 cycles, 615 ops)
_provenance.note: MEASURED, and the shape matters more than any single number. RSS slope is 20.4 kB/cycle over 10 minutes against 1.19 MB/cycle over 45 seconds — a 58x DROP as the run lengthens, which is what warm-up amortizing looks like and NOT what a leak looks like; a leak's per-cycle slope is flat or rising. heapUsed and arrayBuffers both trend NEGATIVE over the long run (GC reclaiming), and open descriptors are bounded (peak 83, spread 24) across 7,245 ops. TWO HONEST CAVEATS. (1) declaredSoakMinutes is 10 because ten minutes is the longest run these ceilings were actually derived from — a genuine multi-day soak has never been executed (see the blocked-external note on #842 W3.4); the weekly lane's multi-hour setting is what turns these into a real distribution. (2) The latency-creep axis is CONFOUNDED BY THE WORKLOAD: every cycle adds three notes and three CAS objects, and the Notes library query the cycle runs reads back the whole notebook, so part of the 1.52x is the vault legitimately getting bigger rather than the gateway getting slower. It is kept because a step change in it is still worth seeing, and the ceiling is sized to allow the workload's own accumulation. A leak-only latency axis needs a fixed-size-corpus cycle and is not yet built. gatewaySqliteSlopeBytesPerCycle (116 kB/cycle, 36 MB -> 158 MB over the run) is PUBLISHED BUT NOT GATED for the same reason — the DB is supposed to grow when the workload writes; a bloat gate needs a bytes-per-committed-write normalisation this rig does not yet compute.
_provenance.headroom: latency creep ~2x the worst observed (1.70); RSS slope ~3.2x the 10-minute observation (a 45-second run is warm-up-dominated and would breach it, which is exactly why the growth ceilings only assert at or above declaredSoakMinutes); descriptors ~3x peak and ~4x spread. Tighten-only.

stressRecovery.volume: the first ordinary app-handler query issued after a concurrency ladder of 1/2/4/8/16/32/64/128 and a 64-wide create-note write storm have all settled — an empty vault with the eight bundled apps installed

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container under sibling agent load; node v22.22.2; WORKER_MAX_CONCURRENT resolves to 2 because isConstrainedWorkerHost() classifies a 4-core host as constrained
_provenance.note: MEASURED. THE KNEE IS EXACTLY WHERE THE CODE SAYS IT SHOULD BE, and that is the finding: 18 requests are admitted and every one beyond that is refused with `503 GATEWAY_BUSY`, which is WORKER_MAX_CONCURRENT (2 on this constrained host) + WORKER_MAX_QUEUE (16) from packages/server/src/engine/handlers/worker-admission.ts. It was identical across all four runs. On a standard host the resolver gives 8 + 16 = 24, so the knee moves one rung but the shape does not. The failure mode is clean in every dimension the rig checks: no untyped refusal, no status outside 429/503, no dropped connection, `PRAGMA integrity_check` ok, and the vault holds EXACTLY as many notes as there were 2xx responses (18 of 64 in the write storm) — a refused write leaves nothing behind. Recovery is immediate: the very next request after the load drops returns 200 in ~0.2 s, so the gateway does not stay wedged behind the surge.
_provenance.headroom: ~3.6x the worst observed (274 ms). Sized against the contended container measurement; tighten-only.

_provenance.note: MEASURED by the #659 vault agent on a real run; cited, not re-derived. This is the audit's worst find (an hourly O(n^2) clustering pass) now bounded at the declared year-3 photo volume. It is a background sweep, so the owner-facing symptom is battery and a hot fan rather than a stalled screen — but at O(n^2) it was a stalled gateway.

photoSemanticSearchAtYear3.volume: 90,000 media assets each carrying one 512-float `embed-image` embedding (184 MB of float32), 8 planted near-matches in the middle of the insert order
photoSemanticSearchAtYear3.probe: tests/scale/photo-similarity.scale.test.ts — ranks the SAME library through BOTH shipping engines (sqlite-vec's vec_distance_cosine and the vault's vault_cosine scalar) and asserts they agree on the top hit before it consults a ceiling. IN the span: the embedding scan, the ranking, the trashed-asset filter over the candidate window, and the wire mapping. OUT of it: embedding the owner's QUERY text, which is the `embed-text` automation's time and not the search's.
photoSemanticSearchAtYear3._ruling: docs/decisions.md Q12 — the vector engine for photo similarity is decided by this rig's numbers, not by a preference. The SQL sqlite-vec floor ranks 90,000 embeddings in 166-243 ms, comfortably inside an interactive ceiling, so a `vec0` ANN index is NOT adopted: it has not been earned. The day either engine goes red here, it has been.

_provenance.host: linux x64, 4 vCPU, 15.7 GiB RAM, shared dev container; node v22.22.2; sqlite-vec v0.1.9 loaded through the gateway's loadExtensions seam
_provenance.note: MEASURED, four implementations against one 90,000 x 512 fixture, isolated from the searchPhotosByText wrapper so the numbers compare like with like. BEFORE — one-stage vec ranking that JOINed media_asset for every embedding: 204.1 / 204.7 ms. AFTER — two-stage vec ranking that joins only the 500-candidate window: 175.3 / 166.6 ms. BEFORE — the unbounded JS scan this wave deleted (every row read into JS, one object each, a 90,000-element Array.sort, then slice 20): 1,059.2 / 1,037.7 ms at +57.5 MiB RSS on the pass that paid for it. AFTER — the same exact cosine computed inside SQLite through vault_cosine with ORDER BY ... LIMIT: 1,010.4 / 934.4 ms at +2.6 / +4.3 MiB, while returning 500 candidates rather than 20. The fallback's TIME is unchanged within noise and this record says so rather than claiming a speedup: both are dominated by 90,000 x 512 float multiplications, which is the work an exact cosine is. What changed is what gets MATERIALISED. Through the full searchPhotosByText wrapper the rig measures 229-243 ms (vec) and 1,204-1,208 ms (fallback); the wrapper adds an index-count and, on the fallback, the per-candidate trashed-asset probes.
_provenance.headroom: ~3x the worst observed for each engine, the same convention the neighbouring entries use for a single contended-host measurement. Tighten-only.
_provenance.rssCaveat: ceilingRssDeltaBytes is COARSE ON PURPOSE. RSS delta across one synchronous call measures GC scheduling as much as allocation — the same fallback search measured +2.6 MiB, +4.3 MiB and +66 MiB on different runs, and the vec engine measures +0 MiB because it allocates nothing in JS. 128 MiB is a `does not materialise the library` bound (the 90,000 x 2 KiB vectors are 184 MiB), not a tight budget. Read the wall clock for cost.
